draft.title: Stone tools and technology
card: First Nations Australians made many tools from stone, wood, bone and shell. Stone tools show the skills and knowledge of people who lived here long ago.
Ground-edge axe
a stone axe with its edge ground smooth and sharp. Some found in northern Australia are among the oldest known in the world.
Grindstone
a flat stone used with a smaller stone to grind seeds into flour. It shows that people gathered seeds and prepared them as food.
Hafted tool
a tool with a stone piece fixed to a handle, often with resin or gum. The handle gives more grip and power.
draft.remember: Ground-edge axes, grindstones and hafted tools show skill in using stone to meet daily needs.

a.q: Archaeologists find a flat stone and a smaller stone with worn, smooth surfaces. What was this pair most likely used for?
opts: Grinding seeds into flour
Fixing a stone blade to a handle
Cutting trees with a sharp edge
Trapping fish in a channel
a.why: A flat stone used with a smaller stone is a grindstone, which was used to grind seeds. Fixing a blade to a handle describes a hafted tool, which does not need a flat grinding surface.
a.clue: Think about preparing seeds as food.

b.q: Mia sees a museum tool with a sharp stone piece fixed to a wooden handle by resin. What kind of tool is this?
opts: A hafted tool
A ground-edge axe
A grindstone
A fishing weir
b.why: A stone piece fixed to a handle is a hafted tool. A ground-edge axe is named for its smooth, sharp edge, and the tool described is defined by its handle instead.
b.clue: Look at how the stone is joined to the handle.

problems.detail: The clue 'Think about preparing seeds as food' gives the answer away. 'Grinding seeds into flour' is the only option that mentions seeds, so students can match words without knowing what a grindstone is.

Ground-edge axes were often hafted, but the card presents them and hafted tools as separate kinds. A student who knows that an axe head is usually fixed to a handle could hesitate over 'A ground-edge axe'. The description gives no ground edge, so the hafted tool is still the best answer, but the overlap is left unexplained.

check.summary: The facts check out and both intended answers are right. The clue for question a gives the answer away, and question b could confuse students because ground-edge axes were themselves often hafted.

proposal.title: Stone tools and technology
card: First Nations Australians made many tools from stone, wood, bone and shell. Stone tools show the skills and knowledge of people who lived here long ago.
Ground-edge axe
a stone axe head with its edge ground smooth and sharp. Some found in northern Australia are among the oldest known in the world.
Grindstone
a flat stone used with a smaller stone to grind seeds into flour. It shows that people gathered seeds and prepared them as food.
Hafted tool
a tool with a stone piece fixed to a handle, often with resin, gum or string. Many ground-edge axe heads were hafted, so one tool can be both.
proposal.remember: Grindstones turned seeds into food, ground edges made axes sharp, and handles added grip and power.

a.q: Archaeologists find a flat stone and a smaller stone with worn, smooth surfaces. What was this pair most likely used for?
opts: Grinding seeds into flour
Fixing a stone blade to a handle
Cutting wood with a sharp edge
Holding a blade in place with gum
a.why: A flat stone used with a smaller stone is a grindstone, which was used to grind seeds into flour. Fixing a blade to a handle describes a hafted tool, which is a single tool with a handle, not a pair of stones.
a.clue: Which tool on the card uses two stones together?

b.q: An axe head with a smooth, ground edge is found tied to a wooden handle with string. Which statement is correct?
opts: It is a ground-edge axe and also a hafted tool
It is a ground-edge axe, so it is not hafted
It is a hafted tool, so its edge was not ground
It is a grindstone, because its edge was ground
b.why: Its ground edge makes it a ground-edge axe, and being fixed to a handle makes it a hafted tool. The two types overlap, since many ground-edge axe heads were hafted, so calling it only one of them is wrong.
b.clue: Check the edge and the handle separately.
